claims.text: The as-synthesized equimolar platinum-group high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are random solid-solution catalysts.
Annealing at 350 °C for calibrated durations induces partial atomic ordering.
The proposed 350 °C annealing treatments can induce ordering while avoiding sintering.
Partial atomic ordering modifies surface strain and local atomic configurations.
Annealing-induced atomic ordering shifts the nanoparticles' d-band center.
A shift in the d-band center tunes the adsorption and desorption kinetics of ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
Tuned adsorption and desorption improve the efficiency of the electron- and proton-transfer steps in ethanol oxidation.
Ethanol oxidation involves a complex 12-electron and 12-proton transfer process.
A moderate degree of atomic ordering increases catalytic activity relative to the disordered baseline.
A moderate degree of atomic ordering enhances selectivity toward complete ethanol-oxidation products.
A moderate degree of atomic ordering improves catalyst durability.
Excessive annealing can cause excessive ordering and nanoparticle sintering.
Annealing-induced sintering reduces catalyst surface area.
Surface-area loss from excessive annealing can eliminate the predicted catalytic benefits.
Ordering can be identified through XRD peak splitting, additional ordering peaks, or electron diffraction.
The d-band center and its shifts can be measured using XPS and in situ spectroscopy.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that performance degradation after excessive annealing and sintering is an expected failure regime outside the proposed mechanism, whereas the falsification rule treats that same degradation as falsification. An anticipated boundary-condition failure does not by itself falsify the moderate-ordering hypothesis.
